canonical_statement: The WHO/ISFC task force was convened to assess the state of the art of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism for medical and other health-related professions.
The WHO and ISFC convened a pulmonary embolism task force in Geneva, Switzerland.
Task-force members prepared position papers and brief oral presentations, then contributed report sections in their areas of expertise.
The report was revised during the Geneva meeting and during subsequent months.
The final report was approved by the WHO-ISFC Task Force on Pulmonary Embolism Steering Committee.
The task force called for more quantitative information on venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism among hospitalized medical patients and high-risk outpatients.
The task force recommended population studies of incidence, survival, and long-term complications across regions with attention to gender and race.
The task force called for greater educational efforts to improve awareness of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism prophylaxis.
The task force identified research on effective methods for changing physician practice as a priority.
Venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism were described as common cardiopulmonary illnesses in North America and Europe.
The report states that pulmonary embolism death rates in the United States were higher in men than women and in nonwhite than white populations.
Pulmonary embolism deaths were described as occurring more frequently with increasing age in North America and Europe.

Contemporary autopsy studies were interpreted as showing that pulmonary embolism remained underdiagnosed in hospitalized patients, especially in older patients and those with underlying cardiopulmonary disease.
Population-based estimates of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism were available from only a few countries and were difficult to compare because diagnostic codes and criteria differed.
The task force called for clear criteria and simple protocols for assessing venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in population studies.

The report lists surgery, trauma, immobilization, cancer, pregnancy or oral contraceptive use, obesity, advanced age, and lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin antibodies as acquired conditions associated with pulmonary embolism.
The report lists antithrombin III deficiency, protein C deficiency, protein S deficiency, and excessive plasminogen activator inhibitor as primary hypercoagulable states.
The report states that thrombotic pulmonary emboli most often embolize to the lower lung lobes, whereas primary thrombosis of pulmonary vessels is found more often in the upper lobes.
Autopsy and follow-up studies were interpreted as showing that postoperative venous thromboembolism risk persists for about one month after surgery or hospital discharge.
The report states that one Geneva study calculated a 30% increase in the postoperative pulmonary embolism rate when events occurring within 30 days after discharge were included.

population.label: Postoperative patients in the Geneva study reported by the task force

concept.text: Including pulmonary emboli occurring within 30 days after hospital discharge

quantitative_result.effect_measure: relative increase in reported postoperative PE rate (%)

canonical_statement: A Swedish autopsy study was summarized as finding no overall change in venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism incidence over a 30-year period, with a decrease in autopsy-proved fatal pulmonary embolism among orthopedic surgical patients but not other groups.
The task force noted that an aging population could mask beneficial effects of prophylaxis in long-term autopsy trends and called for age-corrected prevalence analyses.

The task force called for population studies of incidence, survival, and long-term complications of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism across world regions, including gender- and race-specific comparisons.
The task force suggested reevaluating isolated calf-vein thrombosis and upper-extremity thrombosis as possible antecedents of pulmonary embolism.
The task force suggested that basic thrombosis research could help identify treatable hypercoagulable states among patients with venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
The task force states that clinical suspicion is a prerequisite for diagnosing pulmonary embolism.
Clinical assessment for suspected pulmonary embolism should include signs of venous thrombosis, symptoms such as sudden dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain, and predisposing conditions.

Chest radiography and electrocardiography may support the differential diagnosis in suspected pulmonary embolism, whereas arterial blood gas testing was not recommended as a diagnostic screening test.

The report summarizes PIOPED data as showing no difference in room-air oxygen tension or alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient between angiography-positive and angiography-negative patients without preexisting cardiopulmonary disease.
Chronic pulmonary embolism should be considered as a potentially treatable cause in patients presenting with chronic cor pulmonale.

The task force reports that plasma D-dimer measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay had about 95% sensitivity and could be useful for excluding venous thrombosis, while a positive result required confirmation with more specific testing.

population.label: Patients undergoing diagnostic evaluation for venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism

concept.text: Plasma D-dimer by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay

canonical_statement: When available and feasible, ventilation-perfusion lung scanning should be the primary screening technique for patients with histories suspicious for pulmonary embolism.
A properly performed normal ventilation-perfusion scan was described as effectively ruling out significant pulmonary embolism.

High-probability ventilation-perfusion scans were reported to predict pulmonary embolism accurately in approximately 90% of affected patients and could be accepted as definitive when alternative diagnoses were unlikely.

population.label: Patients evaluated for suspected pulmonary embolism

canonical_statement: Intermediate-probability ventilation-perfusion scans require additional testing to support or exclude venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
If ventilation imaging is unavailable, perfusion scanning interpreted with the chest radiograph may be used, although the report notes that this approach is less standardized.
The task force stated that definitive sensitivity and specificity data for echocardiography in acute pulmonary embolism were not available.

In selected patients with high clinical suspicion, direct echocardiographic visualization of right-sided or proximal pulmonary arterial thrombi together with acute right-ventricular overload may justify prompt treatment when other diagnostic methods are unavailable or contraindicated.

Noninvasive testing of proximal leg veins has an adjunctive role in suspected pulmonary embolism, and a confirmed proximal venous thrombosis may have the same therapeutic implications even though it does not prove pulmonary embolism.
A negative noninvasive or venographic leg examination cannot exclude pulmonary embolism, so additional diagnostic studies are required when suspicion remains.

In hypotensive patients, pulmonary embolism should be suspected when venous thrombosis risk or evidence coexists with clinical evidence of acute cor pulmonale, especially with supportive electrocardiographic findings.

When feasible in hypotensive patients, pulmonary embolism should be confirmed by pulmonary angiography or supported by ventilation-perfusion scanning or echocardiography, with test sequencing determined by local capabilities.
A constant intraluminal filling defect seen in more than one projection was identified as the most reliable pulmonary angiographic feature of pulmonary embolism.
The task force states that properly performed pulmonary angiography can be accomplished with a death rate no higher than 2 to 5 per 1000 procedures.

population.label: Patients undergoing pulmonary angiography for suspected pulmonary embolism

quantitative_result.effect_measure: reported deaths per 1000 procedures (upper bound used as estimate)

canonical_statement: Pulmonary angiography safety measures described by the task force include right-heart catheterization before dye injection, hemodynamic optimization, flexible side-hole or balloon catheters, selective angiography, lower-osmolar contrast, and immediate pressure monitoring.
The task force identified a major need for a noninvasive, accurate, inexpensive diagnostic test for venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

Fiberoptic pulmonary angioscopy and intravascular pulmonary ultrasound were described as potentially useful for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, while additional imaging technologies were considered promising but financially limited.

The task force reports a randomized trial of 35 patients with pulmonary embolism in which recurrent pulmonary embolism occurred in 0 of 16 heparin-treated patients and 10 of 19 placebo-treated patients; five placebo recurrences were fatal.

population.label: Patients with pulmonary embolism in the randomized heparin-versus-placebo trial reported by the task force

quantitative_result.effect_measure: recurrent PE events in placebo arm

canonical_statement: Based on the cited randomized evidence, the task force considered heparin anticoagulation fundamental therapy for most patients with pulmonary embolism.
For hemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism, the report presents either anticoagulation alone or thrombolytic therapy plus anticoagulation as treatment options.
The task force identifies baseline thrombocytopenia, older age, underlying disease, and concomitant drug therapy as factors that may increase bleeding risk during heparin therapy.
Heparin therapy was described as potentially causing a benign thrombocytopenia and, rarely, a life-threatening thrombocytopenia associated with paradoxical arterial thrombosis.
For acute pulmonary embolism, the task force recommends initial intravenous heparin as a bolus followed by continuous infusion, noting that many patients require large doses.

exposures.details: Initial bolus followed by continuous infusion

canonical_statement: The task force states that the activated partial thromboplastin time should ordinarily be maintained at 1.5 to 2.5 times control during heparin treatment.

Before thrombolysis, the report emphasizes careful history and physical examination for bleeding risk because no laboratory test was available to predict thrombolytic bleeding complications in advance.

In patients with high clinical suspicion plus a high-probability lung scan or echocardiographic evidence of central or right-heart thrombus, thrombolysis may be started without angiographic confirmation.

The task force recommends administering thrombolytic therapy through a peripheral vein rather than a pulmonary artery catheter because the latter route was described as neither safer nor more effective.
For hemodynamic instability due to pulmonary embolism, the task force advises considering heparin and/or thrombolysis, vasopressor support such as norepinephrine, and hemodynamic monitoring.
If systemic arterial pressure does not stabilize promptly despite thrombolysis, pulmonary embolectomy may be used in selected patients.
Long-term anticoagulation is prescribed to prevent recurrent venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and is ordinarily achieved with oral anticoagulation.

The report describes pregnancy, prior oral-anticoagulant failure, and selected cancer-associated thrombosis as circumstances in which long-term high-dose subcutaneous heparin may be used instead of oral anticoagulation.
When oral anticoagulation is initiated for pulmonary embolism, the task force recommends overlapping heparin and oral anticoagulation for 4 or 5 days to counter the early decline in protein C.

The task force recommends reporting prothrombin-time monitoring as the international normalized ratio rather than raw prothrombin time or prothrombin-time ratio because thromboplastin sensitivity differs across laboratories.

For oral anticoagulation after pulmonary embolism, the task force gives a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 and states that heparin overlap should continue for at least 4 days even if the INR target is reached sooner.
Oral anticoagulation was generally recommended for at least 3 to 6 months and potentially indefinitely when major underlying risk factors remained uncontrolled.
For patients unable to tolerate heparin or oral anticoagulation, the task force recommends insertion of an inferior vena cava filter.
The report states that pulmonary thromboendarterectomy for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension had a 13% mortality rate under optimal circumstances.

population.label: Patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension undergoing pulmonary thromboendarterectomy

canonical_statement: The task force identified the roles of low-molecular-weight heparins, newer antithrombin agents such as hirudin, and pulmonary embolectomy as unresolved treatment questions.
The task force states that pulmonary embolism is easier and less expensive to prevent than to diagnose and treat.

Table 3 organizes nonpharmacologic prophylaxis as graduated compression stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression, inferior vena cava interruption, combined nonpharmacologic methods, and combined nonpharmacologic plus pharmacologic approaches.

Table 4 lists unfractionated low-dose subcutaneous heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, dextran, adjusted-dose warfarin for orthopedic surgery, and very-low-dose warfarin as pharmacologic prophylaxis options.

Table 5 recommends combined intermittent pneumatic compression and pharmacologic prophylaxis for lower-extremity orthopedic surgery, intensive prophylaxis for gynecologic cancer surgery, combined approaches for general surgery, and nonpharmacologic or pharmacologic prophylaxis for immobilized medical patients.

The task force recommends venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for virtually all hospitalized adults, particularly after major surgery, and for women after delivery, with modality selected according to risk.
Because venous thromboembolism risk persists after hospital discharge, the task force recommends continuing prophylaxis at home for patients at moderate or high risk.

The report describes graduated compression stockings that typically provide approximately 18 mm Hg at the ankle, 14 mm Hg at the calf, 8 mm Hg at the knee, 10 mm Hg at the lower thigh, and 8 mm Hg at mid-thigh.

exposures.details: Approximate compression profile: ankle 18 mm Hg; calf 14; knee 8; lower thigh 10; mid-thigh 8

canonical_statement: Graduated compression stockings were recommended as first-line pulmonary embolism prophylaxis for hospitalized patients except those with peripheral arterial disease, with attention to avoiding a proximal tourniquet effect.

Intermittent pneumatic compression was described as preventing venous stasis and stimulating endogenous fibrinolysis; sequential pressures of about 35, 30, and 20 mm Hg at ankle, calf, and thigh were reported to more than double peak leg blood-flow velocity.

exposures.details: Sequential gradient compression around 35/30/20 mm Hg at ankle/calf/thigh

canonical_statement: The report lists contraindication to anticoagulation, failure of anticoagulation, and selected extremely high-risk prophylactic situations as the three main indications for inferior vena cava interruption.
The task force favors a multidisciplinary, specifically trained team for vena cava filter selection and placement and calls for additional prospective studies and retrievable-filter development.

A randomized general-surgery trial was summarized as finding graduated compression stockings plus intermittent pneumatic compression more effective than intermittent pneumatic compression alone for preventing venous thrombosis.
Multiple general-surgery studies were summarized as showing graduated compression stockings plus low-dose heparin more effective than low-dose heparin alone for reducing venous thrombosis.

In a meta-analysis of 45 randomized prophylaxis trials in general-surgery patients without cancer, intermittent pneumatic compression plus graduated compression stockings was reported to have a postoperative deep-venous-thrombosis rate of 4.5% (95% CI, 1.1% to 8.0%).

population.label: General-surgery patients without cancer in a meta-analysis of 45 randomized prophylaxis trials

concept.text: Intermittent pneumatic compression plus graduated compression stockings

canonical_statement: In the same meta-analysis, graduated compression stockings plus low-dose heparin was reported to have a postoperative deep-venous-thrombosis rate of 6.3% (95% CI, 0% to 17.6%).

population.label: General-surgery patients without cancer in a meta-analysis of 45 randomized prophylaxis trials

concept.text: Graduated compression stockings plus low-dose heparin

canonical_statement: The International Multicentre Trial regimen summarized by the task force used unfractionated heparin 5000 units subcutaneously 2 hours before elective major surgery and every 8 hours thereafter for 7 days.
The International Multicentre Trial included 4121 patients and the report states that fatal pulmonary embolism was found in 16 control patients versus 2 patients assigned to low-dose heparin.

population.label: Patients older than 40 years scheduled for elective major surgery in the International Multicentre Trial

quantitative_result.effect_measure: fatal PE deaths in heparin arm

canonical_statement: In the International Multicentre Trial summary, low-dose heparin increased wound hematomas but did not increase deaths due to hemorrhage.
A review of 78 randomized trials involving 15,598 patients was summarized as showing a 40% reduction in nonfatal pulmonary embolism with perioperative subcutaneous heparin.

population.label: Patients in 78 randomized perioperative heparin prophylaxis trials

canonical_statement: The same 78-trial review was summarized as showing a 64% reduction in fatal pulmonary embolism with perioperative subcutaneous heparin.

population.label: Patients in 78 randomized perioperative heparin prophylaxis trials

canonical_statement: The report states that excessive bleeding was more common with heparin prophylaxis in the reviewed trials, especially in urologic surgery, but the absolute excess was about 2%.

population.label: Patients in randomized perioperative heparin prophylaxis trials

canonical_statement: The task force describes three potential advantages of low-molecular-weight heparin over unfractionated heparin for prophylaxis: less bleeding, once-daily dosing, and greater efficacy.

A double-blind British study of 295 elective major abdominal-surgery patients was summarized as finding deep venous thrombosis in 2.5% with low-molecular-weight heparin versus 7.5% with unfractionated heparin (P<.05).

population.label: Patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery in the reported double-blind British study

concept.text: Deep venous thrombosis detected by iodine-125 fibrinogen leg scanning

canonical_statement: A meta-analysis was summarized as finding a 20% lower venous-thrombosis rate with low-molecular-weight heparin prophylaxis.

population.label: Patients included in the reported meta-analysis of low-molecular-weight heparin prophylaxis

canonical_statement: The task force notes that different low-molecular-weight heparins have distinct pharmacologic profiles and should be standardized against the WHO-endorsed low-molecular-weight heparin standard.
Dextran was described as potentially causing anaphylaxis, volume overload, nephrotoxicity, and paradoxical bleeding.

Dextran was positioned as a prophylaxis option mainly for patients who need pharmacologic prophylaxis but cannot receive heparin because of bleeding or other heparin adverse reactions such as heparin-associated thrombocytopenia.
In a randomized hip-fracture-surgery trial, adjusted-dose warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 2.7 was reported to reduce venous thrombosis to 20% versus 46% with placebo.

population.label: Patients undergoing surgery for hip fracture in the reported randomized trial

canonical_statement: Fixed very-low-dose warfarin was described as 1 mg daily; the task force states that further trials were needed before recommending this strategy.

In a randomized total-hip-replacement trial, sequential intermittent pneumatic compression and adjusted low-dose warfarin were reported to have equal venographically confirmed deep-venous-thrombosis rates of 17%.

population.label: Patients undergoing total hip replacement in the reported randomized trial

canonical_statement: A more recent total-hip-replacement study was summarized as finding venographically confirmed deep-venous-thrombosis rates of 27% with intermittent pneumatic compression and 31% with warfarin prophylaxis.

population.label: Patients undergoing total hip replacement in the reported comparative study

canonical_statement: For major orthopedic surgery, the task force recommends combined nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic prophylaxis during hospitalization followed by prophylaxis for approximately one month after discharge, with predischarge ultrasonography presented as an alternative strategy.

For gynecologic cancer surgery, the task force recommends intermittent pneumatic compression when nonpharmacologic prophylaxis is chosen and intensive fixed low-dose heparin 5000 units subcutaneously three times daily when pharmacologic prophylaxis is chosen.
Among bedridden patients in a respiratory intensive care unit, one study was summarized as finding pulmonary embolism at autopsy in 27%, with half of those emboli not diagnosed before death.

population.label: Bedridden patients in a respiratory intensive care unit in the reported study

canonical_statement: A second study of immobilized noncritically ill patients was summarized as finding deep venous thrombosis in 13% by fibrinogen leg scanning.

population.label: Immobilized noncritically ill patients in the reported study

canonical_statement: The task force concludes that immobilized medical patients should routinely receive nonpharmacologic or pharmacologic venous-thromboembolism prophylaxis.

Economic analyses cited by the report found that prophylaxis saved health-care costs in major orthopedic surgery and that graduated compression stockings were the most cost-effective approach in general surgery.
The task force describes specific antithrombin drugs such as hirudin as promising agents for preventing venous thrombosis.
The task force concludes that venous-thromboembolism prophylaxis was underused despite effective nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic methods.
The task force endorses intensified prophylaxis for high-risk patients during hospitalization and through the first month after discharge.

The task force recommends that clinicians review institutional thromboprophylaxis policy, assess venous-thromboembolism risk for every hospitalized patient, and use safeguards to ensure appropriate prophylaxis for high-risk patients.
